The Treaty of Tordesillas was indeed signed on June 7, 1494 to resolve territorial disputes between Spain and Portugal concerning newly discovered lands outside Europe following Columbus's voyages. Certainly! The Treaty of Tordesillas was a significant agreement between Spain and Portugal that aimed to resolve the territorial disputes over newly discovered lands outside Europe by Christopher Columbus and other late 15th-century voyagers. Signed on June 7, 1494, this treaty involved drawing an imaginary line from pole to pole in the Atlantic Ocean, with all new territories found west of that line belonging to Spain and those to the east to Portugal.

The treaty was brokered by Pope Alexander VI who issued papal bulls that granted rights over newly discovered lands but led to conflict between these two major sea powers. The Treaty of Tordesillas aimed at preventing further disputes by clearly demarcating zones of influence for both countries, although the line itself was not strictly respected by other nations and led to later conflicts, particularly in the New World where France and England also sought territories that were now considered Spanish or Portuguese.

The signing of this treaty marked a key moment in colonial history, shaping the linguistic, cultural, and political landscapes of many countries in South America. The Treaty remained significant until it was eventually superseded by other agreements as new nations emerged from European colonies.
